checkpoints: Calling `ZADD` unconditionally, before the `count < limit` check even runs, means the sorted set records every request that hits the key — accepted and rejected alike — instead of only the ones that actually consume quota.

When a client is flooded far past its limit, that unconditional `ZADD` keeps writing one new member per attempt into the ZSET regardless of the reject decision, so the set's memory footprint scales with total attempts rather than with the configured `limit`.
The count check itself is correct — it does gate the allow/reject decision properly — the bug is purely in the bookkeeping that happens one line earlier and independently of that decision.

The fix is to move `ZADD` inside the branch where `count < limit`, so the sorted set only gains a member when a request is actually granted, and to return early on the reject path without touching the ZSET at all.

Restructuring around a 'record-on-grant' rule bounds the ZSET to roughly `limit` entries per active client, since denied requests never get written, no matter how many times an abusive client retries.

The key also has no `PEXPIRE`, so a legitimate client that sends a few requests and then goes silent leaves its ZSET sitting in Redis forever — nothing ever reclaims it because `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` only trims on the next call to that key, which never comes.
Calling `PEXPIRE(key, window)` right after every successful `ZADD` makes an idle key self-expire after one window of inactivity, closing the second, independent leak from the record-on-reject bug.

Verifying the fix means flooding one key with far more requests than its limit and asserting the ZSET's cardinality stabilizes near `limit` instead of climbing with the attempt count, then confirming the key's TTL expires it once traffic stops.
